title: A Dead Star Spins Every 8 Minutes and Sends Mysterious Radio Pulses
summary:
Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to a strange pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One of them is a dead star that spins once every eight minutes. Its companion looks a lot like our own Sun.

The discovery comes from researchers at Curtin University's International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research, known as ICRAR. The system, called GPM J071507-114153, holds a white dwarf and a G-type star circling each other. A white dwarf is the dense leftover of a star that has burned through its fuel and shed its outer layers, while its companion belongs to the same family of stars as the Sun.

Until now, astronomers had only seen similar radio pulses in systems pairing a white dwarf with a smaller, cooler red dwarf star. This is the first time such signals have been found in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

The pair belongs to a rare group called long-period transients, or LPTs. These objects send out radio signals that appear and vanish over periods of minutes to hours. The same ICRAR team found the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been spotted since.

This time, the observations were detailed enough to follow the white dwarf as it moved around its companion. That let researchers pinpoint where the pulses likely come from: a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly the white dwarf itself. The team studied more than 100 hours of radio observations to confirm the result.

The signals revealed something else, too. They showed powerful magnetic storms on the Sun-like companion. The team also saw the white dwarf pass behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a stellar prominence — a huge loop of electrically charged gas erupting from the star's surface. Lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney said it is amazing that radio waves can reveal storms on a star so far away.
why_it_matters: Studying these rare pulsing stars helps astronomers understand how dead stars behave, and shows how radio waves can reveal storms on stars far too distant to visit.

background_read: A white dwarf is what remains after a star like our Sun burns through its fuel and sheds its outer layers, leaving a small, dense core.
Some pairs of stars send out radio signals that appear and vanish, and astronomers call these rare objects long-period transients.
Radio telescopes on Earth can pick up these signals, letting scientists study stars thousands of light-years away without ever seeing them with their eyes.
This new system is unusual because its white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star, a pairing never seen sending such pulses before.
